title: Guesstimate Workbook
subtitle: Master Market Sizing and Estimation Questions for Consulting & Strategy Interviews

sections.title: Why Guesstimates Matter in Consulting Interviews

blocks.text: Guesstimates test your ability to **think logically, structure problems, and stay calm under pressure.** Recruiters don’t care if your number is exact—they care about your approach.

items: If asked “Estimate the number of ATMs in India,” a random guess fails. Segmenting logically (population → banked households → ATM demand per household) impresses.

blocks.text: Consulting firms like McKinsey, BCG, and Bain use guesstimates to filter candidates who can **simplify ambiguity into structure.**

blocks.label: Exercise
blocks.text: Write one recent time you had to make a quick estimate at work or in daily life.
MECE = **Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive.** Break problems into non-overlapping parts that together cover the whole.

items: Estimate pizza consumption in India.
list: Break by **size** (small vs medium vs large).

blocks.text: MECE keeps you from double-counting and ensures logical coverage.

blocks.label: Exercise
blocks.text: Pick a guesstimate (e.g., number of Uber rides in Mumbai). Write your MECE breakdown.
Every guesstimate starts with populations. Break them into **manageable, logical buckets.**

items: Number of toothpaste tubes sold annually in India.
list: Average person uses 4 tubes a year, so about 4B tubes annually.

blocks.label: Exercise
blocks.text: Pick 1 consumer good and estimate annual demand in your city.
Assumptions drive estimates. State them clearly.

items: Estimate number of flights landing in Delhi daily.
list: Drivers: Number of passengers, avg. plane capacity, % seat utilization.
If Delhi handles ~200,000 passengers/day, planes average 200 seats, 80% occupancy → ~1,250 flights/day.

blocks.label: Exercise
blocks.text: Write 3 assumptions you’d need to estimate car washes in Mumbai.
Quick math is essential. Round numbers smartly.

items: Instead of 1.38B → 1.4B.

blocks.text: Clarity > Precision. Communicate your math as you go.

blocks.label: Exercise
blocks.text: Estimate the number of coffee cups sold daily at Starbucks in India.
Always sanity check. If your result seems absurd (e.g., “100B pizzas annually in India”), revise assumptions.
Methods:

items: Compare to known data.
Use ratios (“1 ATM per 10,000 people”).
Check per capita feasibility.

blocks.label: Exercise
blocks.text: Pick 1 creative question and build a MECE structure.
A candidate was asked: “Estimate the number of gas stations in Delhi.”

items: Broke Delhi population (~20M) into households.
Assumed 40% own vehicles → ~8M vehicles.
Avg. vehicle fills 40L monthly → 320M liters/month.
Avg. station dispenses 400,000L/month → ~800 stations.

blocks.text: The interviewer cared more about the structure than the final number.

blocks.label: Lesson
blocks.text: Structure > Accuracy.

items: Diving into math without structure.
Forgetting sanity checks.
Freezing under pressure.
